So we're left with a question of what was happening. Pats fans will point out that the videotaping wasn't as serious of a 'crime' as it was represented, to the point that ESPN even issued an apology, WAAAY late, about their representation of the events. However, to me the bigger issue is the idea that Brady and the defensive captain were being told the opposing teams plays ahead of time. From the article: "He was instructed to memorize them, and during the game, to watch Bucs defensive coordinator Monte Kiffin and tell Weis the defensive play, which Weis would relay over the radio headset system to quarterback Drew Bledsoe." This is a big advantage if it is true, even more than simply taping them and knowing them pre-game, knowing them in-game is insane.

But of course, all of this is conjecture. Pats fans are safe to assume innocence, (let's be honest, if it was YOUR team, would you admit guilt at all? Really? You sure?) and I get it. It's something that while I understand the motivation behind Goodell doing what he did, that if the allegations are as true as it sounds, as bad as the punishment was, it still wasn't as bad as the public would have wanted. Literally if everything was true that happened, that the Pats had been cheating with videotapes for 7+ years, stealing pregame play sheets and listening into conversations... the public outcry would have been so bad, that Donald Sterling would have thought he got off light.

It would have been disastrous for the league as a whole, and Goodell being in his first years as a commissioner was not prepared to deal with something like this. Ultimately this article does nothing more than show that the league is inept at dealing with punishing wrong-doing or even investigating it. But destroying evidence will ultimately always be a black spot on Roger Goodell's legacy. It has allowed Pat's fans to claim innocence and Anti-Pat's fans to continue to call them cheaters, without either side knowing what is the real story.
